papers.title: Tear proteomics reveals reproducible pathway-level signatures of Parkinson's disease pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: Tear fluid is a promising minimally invasive biofluid for studying molecular alterations in neurodegenerative diseases. In this exploratory study, we applied a quantitative dia-PASEF nanoLC-MS/MS workflow to profile the tear proteome in idiopathic Parkinson's disease (iPD), LRRK2-associated Parkinson's disease (LRRK2-PD), and healthy controls. Protein identification and quantification were performed using DIA-NN, and statistical analyses were conducted on log₂-transformed data with false discovery rate (FDR) correction using the Storey-Tibshirani method. Tear samples from 77 iPD patients, 7 symptomatic LRRK2 mutation carriers and 86 controls were analysed. iPD showed a broad proteomic shift, with 300 proteins significant after FDR correction and five combining FDR-adjusted significance with large effect sizes. Cross-study comparison with our pilot cohort identified eight concordantly increased proteins significant in both datasets. Exploratory enrichment analysis suggested involvement of epithelial and mucosal homeostasis, innate immunity, cytoskeletal organization, mitochondrial metabolism and endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis. Selected proteins, including MUC5AC, ATPA, KRT19, LCN2 and RARRES1, showed exploratory associations with motor severity and Hoehn and Yahr staging. LRRK2-PD showed nominal changes only. Overall, these findings identify a restricted set of recurrent tear protein candidates in iPD and support further targeted assessment in larger, clinically and genetically stratified cohorts.

papers.title: Glutamate co-release from inhibitory nigral neurons reverses motor deficits in a Parkinson's disease mouse model.
papers.abstract: Degeneration of midbrain dopamine neurons in Parkinson's disease increases inhibitory output from the basal ganglia, including from GABAergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), thereby suppressing thalamocortical drive and impairing movement. Whether altering the transmitter output of these inhibitory neurons can restore circuit function remains unknown. Here, we genetically reprogrammed mouse SNr GABAergic neurons to co-release glutamate by Cre-dependent expression of the vesicular glutamate transporter VGLUT2. VGLUT2 expression was both necessary and sufficient to induce glutamate co-release and activate postsynaptic glutamate receptors in thalamic target neurons. In a mouse model of unilateral dopamine depletion, ectopic VGLUT2 expression robustly restored motor performance. These findings demonstrate that basal ganglia output neurons retain the capacity for functional transmitter reconfiguration and that inducing glutamate co-release in SNr GABA neurons can reverse pathological motor deficits resulting from dopamine denervation.

papers.title: GBA1 mutations as a role model for precision medicine in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Genetic variants in GBA1, encoding the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCase), represent the strongest genetic risk factor for Parkinson's disease (PD) and provide a mechanistic link between Gaucher disease (GD) and PD. While biallelic GBA1 mutations cause GD, heterozygous variants confer an increased, age-dependent risk of PD, with mutation-specific differences in penetrance, age at onset, cognitive decline, and survival. This review critically examines the molecular and clinical spectrum of GBA1-associated PD (GBA1-PD), highlighting the relationship between variant severity, lysosomal dysfunction, and disease progression. We discuss two major, partially overlapping pathogenic frameworks underlying GBA1-PD: loss-of-function mechanisms associated with reduced GCase activity, glycosphingolipid accumulation, and impaired autophagy-lysosomal pathways, and toxic gain-of-function mechanisms driven by mutant GCase misfolding, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and proteostatic imbalance. Increasing evidence suggests that these mechanisms converge on α-synuclein aggregation and dopaminergic neurodegeneration. We further summarize emerging disease-modifying therapeutic strategies, including small-molecule GCase activators, pharmacological chaperones, substrate reduction therapies, acid ceramidase inhibitors, and gene therapies. Although clinical outcomes have been heterogeneous, GBA1-associated PD represents a valuable model for precision medicine, illustrating how genetic stratification can guide mechanism-based therapeutic development in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: State-dependent reconfiguration failure of the basal forebrain-cortical gradient in Parkinson's disease with freezing of gait.
papers.abstract: Accumulating evidence implicates cholinergic dysfunction in freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease (PD). Given the basal forebrain (BF) provides the primary cholinergic input to the cortex, elucidating BF-cortical connectivity and its dynamic reconfiguration during motor challenges in PD-FOG is important. This study included 44 PD-FOG, 45 without FOG (PD-NFOG), and 27 healthy controls (HC). All underwent diffusion and resting-state functional MRI. A subgroup (27 PD-FOG, 20 PD-NFOG, 27 HC) also underwent gait-related task-based fMRI. Multimodal gradients of BF connectivity were compared across the three groups and between task and rest. BF free-water was elevated in both PD groups versus HC. Connectivity gradient analysis further revealed reduced structure-function coupling along the anteromedial-to-posterolateral BF axis, with weakest coupling in posterolateral subregions. Cortically, coupling progressively reduced from unimodal sensory to transmodal association cortex. While this topographic architecture was qualitatively preserved in both PD groups, during turning imagery, PD-FOG patients exhibited impaired adaptive decoupling in the somatomotor network, localized to an insular hub with attenuated task-evoked nodal responsivity. BF free-water elevation and hub dysfunction independently predicted clinical status along the continuum from healthy to PD-NFOG to PD-FOG. Our findings reveal a state-dependent reconfiguration failure in PD-FOG, suggesting a circuit-level, neurodynamic mechanism for FOG.

papers.title: Marked dopaminergic denervation in early stages of Perry syndrome.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Perry Syndrome (PS) is a rare autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the DCTN1 gene. Clinically it is characterized by a combination of parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric symptoms, weight loss, and central hypoventilation. PS patients exhibit a variable response to dopaminergic medications. Dopaminergic imaging in these patients is rarely reported, but signs of presynaptic dopaminergic deficit are expected. CASE REPORT: We report a 43-year-old male with genetically confirmed PS who presented with early parkinsonism and relatively preserved response to levodopa, and before developing respiratory problems and weight loss. Ioflupane I-123 SPECT (DaTSCAN) repeatedly demonstrated nearly complete absence of striatal tracer uptake, a severity not previously described in early stages of the disease. CONCLUSIONS: This finding suggests that marked dopaminergic denervation may be present at an early clinical stage of Perry syndrome, even in patients who respond to levodopa. Whether this reflects dopaminergic involvement preceding more widespread neurodegeneration in the globus pallidus cannot be determined from a single case, and this possibility needs to be confirmed in larger studies.

papers.title: Seed Amplification Assay-Based Detection of Alpha-Synuclein Aggregates Outperforms Immunohistochemical Analysis in the Intestinal Mucosal Biopsies of Parkinson's Disease and Multiple System Atrophy Participants.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine whether an α-synuclein (α-Syn) seed-amplification-assay (SAA) detects seeding-competent aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies, differs by gastrointestinal region, registers pathology more frequently than immunohistochemistry (IHC), and associates with Parkinson's disease (PD) diagnosis, disease duration or severity. DESIGN: This cross-sectional, proof-of-concept diagnostic accuracy study analyzed duodenum, ileum, and sigmoid biopsies from PD participants, age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC), plus exploratory multiple system atrophy (MSA) subtypes [parkinsonian (MSA-P) and cerebellar (MSA-C)]. Ileal and sigmoid PD and HC biopsies were assessed using proteinase K-resistant phospho-Ser129 IHC. SAA-positivity was evaluated against clinical and biological measures. RESULTS: In PD, SAA detected seeding-competent α-Syn aggregates with high observed specificity (97.5-100%) and region-dependent sensitivity (18/37, 48.65% in ileum and 36/56, 64.29% in sigmoid). Sigmoid SAA positivity increased significantly with PD disease duration (40.00% at <5 years, 73.33% at 5-10 years, and 93.75% at >10 years), independent of motor severity, whereas ileal positivity remained stable across disease stages. In 37 paired sigmoid biopsies, SAA detected α-Syn aggregates 2.8-fold more frequently than IHC. Sigmoid seeding activity was detected in all five MSA-P, but not in two MSA-C. IHC did not detect aggregates in any MSA. CONCLUSIONS: In PD, α-Syn SAA detected seeding-competent α-Syn-aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies with high observed specificity, moderate sensitivity, and approximately 2.8-fold higher detection rate than IHC in sigmoid. Positive SAA in MSA patients supports GI involvement across synucleinopathies. SAA detection in PD differed by intestinal region and disease duration, supporting further validation of intestinal SAA as a PD biomarker. papers.title: Path to Prevention Platform Trial in Early-Stage Neuronal Alpha-Synuclein Disease: Study Design.
papers.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.abstract: The development of biologically targeted therapeutics (BTTs) that slow Parkinson's disease progression has been hampered by a reliance on testing interventions in clinically defined populations with already advanced pathobiology. Publications on the biological definition and classification of neuronal ⍰-synuclein disease (NSD), and the development of the NSD integrated staging system (NSD-ISS), have generated a framework for identifying individuals with NSD prior to the emergence of a clinically defined syndrome. Path to Prevention (P2P) is a phase 2A, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled platform trial designed to assess the safety and efficacy of interventions in an early-stage NSD population. The trial is embedded within the observational Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), a structure that enables recruitment of participants from the PPMI cohort, leverages existing operational infrastructure, and utilizes data from non-P2P enrolled PPMI participants in the Bayesian statistical modeling. P2P will enroll participants at least 60 years of age with NSD Stage 2B (abnormal ⍰-synuclein, dopaminergic dysfunction, and prodromal signs or symptoms without functional impairment) without a clinically defined diagnosis of PD or a related disorder. As a platform trial, P2P will enable the testing of multiple interventions under a Master Protocol at approximately 35 sites across North America and Europe. Interventions are selected from industry-submitted applications based on biological relevance of the targets, and on the adequacy of the safety data appropriate to the target population. Each treatment regimen will have 125 participants on active treatment and at least 125 shared placebo control participants. Participants will remain on treatment for a maximum of 144 weeks or until 96 weeks since the randomization of the last participant. papers.title: Statistical design of Path to Prevention platform trial in early neuronal alpha-synuclein disease.
papers.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.abstract: The Path to Prevention (P2P) platform trial is a first-in-class, phase 2A, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled learning study. papers.title: Assessment of Cytotoxicity of α-Synuclein in Budding Yeast Using a Spot Growth Assay and Fluorescent Microscopy.
papers.abstract: The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a model organism amenable to both genetic analysis and cell biology. Due to these advantages, yeast has provided platforms to examine the properties of pathogenic proteins involved in human diseases. The methods used to examine the cytotoxicity and intracellular localization of α-Synuclein, a human neuronal protein implicated in Parkinson's disease, using yeast have been described herein. These methods are readily accessible to researchers or graduate students unfamiliar with experiments using yeast and applicable to larger-scale analyses, such as high-throughput genetic and chemical screenings.

papers.title: Lipidomics in Brain Health and Neurodegenerative Diseases: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Lipids constitute nearly half of the brain's dry weight and play a crucial role in maintaining the function of the central nervous system (CNS). Beyond their well-known function as structural components of cellular membranes and energy storage, lipids are now identified as dynamic bioactive mediators that regulate neuronal signaling, synaptic plasticity, membrane integrity and neuroinflammatory responses. Emerging evidence demonstrates that altered lipid homeostasis is associated with the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington's disease (HD). In this review, we highlight key pathophysiological mechanisms, including dysregulation of lipid transport by cholesterol and apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4), which may influence the aggregation of amyloid-β in AD. We discuss sphingolipid dysregulation and impaired glucocerebrosidase activity in modulating α-synuclein pathology in PD. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and their oxidized forms in the regulation of oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and neuronal cell death in ALS and HD. Besides mechanistic information, this review also highlights the recent advancements in modern lipidomic technologies, such as high-resolution mass spectrometry and multi-omics integration, which have facilitated the comprehensive characterization of disease-associated lipid alterations. Emerging lipid signatures, including alterations in ceramide, cholesterol metabolism and lipid droplet biogenesis in glial cells, are being investigated as candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Collectively, we outline a strategy for exploiting the brain lipidome to explore the potential for personalized disease-modifying strategies against neurodegeneration by integrating mechanistic, diagnostic and therapeutic insights.

papers.title: Bypassing the Blood-Brain Barrier: A Dual-Axis Framework for Parkinson's Disease Utilizing Glymphatic-Lymphatic Clearance and In Situ Chaperone Synthesis.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized neuropathologically by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and by aggregation of misfolded alpha-synuclein into Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, which is proposed to propagate in a prion-like manner following a stereotyped, stage-dependent pattern described by Braak staging. Because any circulating agent intended to act within the central nervous system (CNS) must cross the blood-brain barrier, this review proposes active craniospinal tensioning (ACT), a mechanical, non-pharmacological route to disease modification acting on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and cerebral venous pressure dynamics. ACT combines two concurrent mechanisms converging on a single venous-side target within Monro-Kellie/Queckenstedt pressure continuity: suboccipital venous occlusion-rebound, proposed to raise and release craniospinal CSF pressure to accelerate venous-side glymphatic efflux, and dural pull-recoil, a reverse Queckenstedt effect in which spinal elongation is proposed to generate a CSF-side pressure gradient with a coupled venous component. The proposed disease-modifying route is clearance of transiting extracellular alpha-synuclein from the perivascular and interstitial space before it templates a neighboring cell. The claim is scoped to the CNS phase of PD, excluding peripheral vagal or olfactory transport, with its most direct anatomical rationale at the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV), one of the two earliest CNS sites of Lewy pathology in Braak staging and adjacent to ACT's craniocervical site of action, where ACT is proposed to act on onward extracellular spread rather than on arrival. A secondary, hypothesis-generating axis, cerebral venous preconditioning (CVPC), proposes that the same cycle produces venule- and capillary-wall strain sufficient to activate heat shock factor 1 (HSF-1) within the neurovascular unit, beginning at the vessel wall, independent of oxygen tension, with a possible contributi

papers.title: Therapeutic potential of gastrodin in Parkinson's disease: mechanistic insights into the Nrf2/ARE, p38 MAPK, and Bax/Bad signaling pathways.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive, neurodegenerative condition that results in selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, resulting in a loss of dopamine and debilitating motor and non-motor symptoms. The multi-faceted nature of PD demonstrates the need for multi-target therapeutic strategies that can reduce the disease process; these include oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, α-synuclein aggregation and neuronal apoptosis. The main phenolic glycoside compound obtained from Gastrodia elata Blume is called gastrodin, which is 4-hydroxybenzyl alcohol-4-O-β-D-glucopyranoside, and it has also been identified as a phytochemical with great potential as a neuroprotective compound due to its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial protective properties. In this review, we summarized the molecular mechanisms responsible for the neuroprotective actions of gastrodin in experimental models of PD, including the Keap1-Nrf2/ARE, the ROS-mediated p38 MAPK/JNK/ERK inflammatory signaling pathway, and the mitochondrial Bax/Bcl-2/Bad/caspase apoptotic pathway. Gastrodin is an Nrf2 inducer that can induce Nrf2-dependent antioxidant enzyme transcription, such as HO-1, NQO1, SOD, CAT and GSH, and thus reduce oxidative stress and maintain mitochondrial function. Besides, it inhibits ROS-induced activation of p38 MAPK, JNK and ERK, thereby depressing the activation of microglial cells and the secretion of pro-inflammatory mediators like IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α. Gastrodin also enhances the ratio of Bcl-2 to Bax; inhibits the activation of Bad; prevents cytochrome c release; suppresses the activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3; and prevents neuronal apoptosis. Gastrodin offers significant potential as a multi-target neuroprotective therapeutic agent to develop disease-modifying drugs for PD.

papers.title: Disease aging clocks in the plasma proteome stratify risk and track preclinical progression.
papers.abstract: Aging is the strongest risk factor for most chronic diseases, yet people of the same chronological age differ in how far disease processes have advanced. Existing plasma proteomic clocks estimate chronological age, or the age of a single organ, but none targets the pathway from aging to a specific disease. Here we developed disease aging clocks by deriving the plasma proteomic composite that maximizes the age-mediated component of disease risk and applied the framework to 31 age-related diseases in 44,526 UK Biobank participants. The resulting disease age gap separated 10-year incidence up to 20-fold among individuals of the same chronological age, and each additional year of gap raised the hazard of type 2 diabetes by 24%, chronic kidney disease by 21% and Alzheimer's disease (AD) by 17%. Among participants who went on to develop disease, the gap was larger closer to diagnosis in 19 of 20 diseases, indicating that it reports preclinical stage rather than fixed susceptibility. Across these 20 diseases, 56% of the gap was orthogonal to chronological and organ-specific clocks. Applied without refitting to Stanford Alzheimer's Disease Research Center participants (n=501), the AD clock was elevated in AD and Lewy body disease but not Parkinson's disease, and tracked plasma biomarkers, cognition and neuroimaging features. Disease aging clocks provide a blood-based measure of the stage of a specific aging-to-disease process years before diagnosis, with potential applications in prevention-trial enrichment and longitudinal disease monitoring.

papers.title: Psychosis with continuous delivery of subcutaneous levodopa: importance of the correct patient profile.
papers.abstract: Continuous 24-h subcutaneous infusion of foslevodopa/foscarbidopa (LDp/CDp), a soluble formulation of levodopa prodrugs delivered through a minimally invasive subcutaneous infusion system, is currently available for the management of advanced Parkinson's disease (APD) in many countries. Pivotal licensing studies and open-label studies confirm the efficacy of this first subcutaneous 24-h levodopa delivery option in APD in terms of motor effects, early-morning off periods, and sleep benefits. However, in addition to reports of skin reactions, there are also case report series and case-based concerns regarding neuropsychiatric side effects such as psychosis and hallucinations in some centres. The pattern appears to be either an early or late occurrence of psychosis, often in older patients with significant comorbidities. A critical review of such reports shows that the selected cases might have been vulnerable to psychosis, and potential corrective adjustments to the dosing of LDp/CDp were not evident; in some cases, there were unusual initiation processes. We review the entire published literature on clinical case reports of psychosis and the use of LDp/CDp and provide expert opinion-based tips on correct patient profiling and selection and on avoiding discontinuation of LDp/CDp therapy.

papers.title: Performance-Based Evolution of Near-Infrared Serotonin Nanosensors from DNA-Wrapped Carbon Nanotube Libraries.
papers.abstract: Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5HT) is an important neurotransmitter involved in the regulation of mood, appetite, and sleep, and its dysregulation has been associated with disorders such as depression and Parkinson's disease. Selective molecular tools that can distinguish 5HT from other neurochemicals are essential for advancing both neurochemistry and disease-related research. However, conventional analytical methods are labor-intensive and sometimes suffer from poor discrimination among closely related neurotransmitters. In this study, we developed a near-infrared fluorescent 5HT nanosensor based on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA)-wrapped single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) using a performance-based systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (pSELEC) strategy. Unlike conventional affinity-focused selection, this approach prioritized fluorescence modulation as the screening output and combined high-throughput microarray printing with automated fluorescence imaging to evaluate more than 108 ssDNA-SWCNT configurations. After characterizing the enriched DNA candidates, Seq6 was selected as a lead scaffold and underwent post-selection engineering, including covalent modification with a quencher dye and co-wrapping with spacer ssDNA. A methylene blue-conjugated Seq6 produced a "turn-off" fluorescence response to 5HT together with an opposite-direction response to dopamine (DA), providing improved discrimination between the two analytes. These findings demonstrate that pSELEC is a useful strategy for developing sensitive and selective near-infrared nanosensors for real-time neurotransmitter sensing.

papers.title: Psychobiotics and the Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis: Mechanistic Insights, Multi-Omics Advances, and Therapeutic Potential in Mental and Systemic Disorders.
papers.abstract: Common mental illnesses, such as anxiety, depression, and neurodegenerative diseases, are increasing worldwide, and there is increasing evidence that their pathogenesis is associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis and disruption of the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA). Nevertheless, there is a lack of mechanistic understanding and clinical translation of psychobiotics. This review consolidates the results of preclinical, clinical, and multi-omics research to assess the role of psychobiotics, such as prebiotics, probiotics, synbiotics, and postbiotics, in regulating MGBA pathways, including endocrine, immune, neural, and metabolic pathways, along with developments in metabolite detection and microbial profiling. Psychobiotics normalize the intestinal microbial composition, increase the intestinal barrier integrity, and balance neuroinflammation. They modulate the levels of major neurotransmitters (dopamine, serotonin, γ-aminobutyric acid) and suppress hyperactivity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. There is growing evidence showing their therapeutic efficacy in gastrointestinal, metabolic, autoimmune, and neuropsychiatric diseases, including anxiety, depression, and Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Synergistic effects with neuro-nutrition and physical activity further enhance cognitive function and neuroplasticity. Psychobiotics provide a mechanism-based approach to address interconnected pathways of the MGBA, which is an exciting addition to traditional treatments with an excellent safety profile. Precision psychobiotic intervention and translation of multi-omics approaches into clinical practice require standardized and large-scale clinical trials as well as integration of these methods.

papers.title: Smaller Cortical Responses to Balance Perturbations in Parkinson's Disease with Freezing of Gait.
papers.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) is among the most disabling symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) and is associated with balance impairment and increased falls risk, yet remains challenging to understand due to its episodic and context-dependent nature. Altered supplementary motor area (SMA) function at rest and before self-initiated movements has been implicated in FoG; however, whether this extends to functionally relevant balance behavior is unknown. A loss of balance in response to support surface translations during standing elicits a perturbation-evoked N1 potential, an error assessment signal linked to SMA activity. We therefore predicted that people with FoG would have smaller and later N1 responses than people with PD without FoG and older adults. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) during backward support-surface translations in 29 people with PD (71 ± 7 years), including 13 people with a history of FoG (FoG+) and 16 people without FoG (FoG-), and 26 older adults (OA; 67 ± 6 years). N1 amplitude and latency were quantified at a central midline electrode and defined as the largest negative peak 100-300 ms post-perturbation. N1 responses were similar between OA and FoG-(Δ = 4.0 µV and 2.8 ms, respectively). In contrast, FoG+ had smaller N1 amplitudes than FoG- (Δ = 18.1 µV, p = 0.001) and OA (Δ = 14.1 µV, p = 0.003), and both differences persisted after adjusting for age. FoG+ also had later N1 latencies than OA (Δ = 26.5 ms, p = 0.029), with a similar but non-significant difference versus FoG- (Δ = 23.6 ms, p = 0.091); after adjusting for age, these latency differences were not retained. These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked cortical activity is altered in FoG, potentially reflecting altered SMA function, and may provide a functionally relevant marker of FoG susceptibility.

papers.title: Test-retest reliability and practical suitability of cognitive outcomes for monitoring change in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Cognitive tests are commonly used to evaluate the effects of cognitive and exercise interventions in Parkinson's disease, but their ability to distinguish genuine change from measurement variability remains insufficiently characterized. This study examined the test-retest reliability, measurement error, and practical suitability of executive and related cognitive outcomes in people with Parkinson's disease. Participants completed the same computerized and verbal cognitive battery on two occasions separated by approximately five to six weeks. Relative reliability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients, while absolute reliability was examined using the standard error of measurement, minimal detectable change at the 95% confidence level, systematic between-session change, and Bland-Altman analysis. Phonemic fluency showed the most favorable relative reliability, whereas forward Corsi span demonstrated a consistent agreement profile without marked systematic bias or heteroscedasticity. Trail Making Test Part B accuracy and a parsimonious global cognitive composite showed moderate reliability but required caution because of heteroscedasticity or relatively large detectable-change thresholds. Several working-memory, action-fluency, planning, and card-sorting outcomes showed limited reliability or substantial measurement error. Completion time for the Tower of London improved systematically at retest, indicating a marked familiarization effect. These findings provide preliminary evidence that cognitive measures commonly used in Parkinson's disease differ substantially in their short-term measurement profiles. Given the modest sample and the resulting uncertainty around several intraclass correlation coefficient estimates, the practical classifications should be interpreted as provisional and confirmed in larger independent cohorts. papers.title: Nonlinear Dopaminergic Vulnerability and Incident Freezing of Gait in Parkinson Disease: Limited Incremental Value of Global Volumetric MRI.
papers.abstract: Freezing of gait is a disabling manifestation of Parkinson disease, but it remains uncertain how risk varies across the spectrum of nigrostriatal dopaminergic loss and whether global volumetric magnetic resonance imaging adds prognostic information. We analyzed longitudinal Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative data from participants who remained free of recorded freezing through completion of a temporally aligned multimodal imaging index. The cohort comprised 521 participants with 251 incident recorded events; 520 participants and 250 events contributed to adjusted models. Lower mean striatal specific binding ratio was associated with subsequent recorded freezing after adjustment for age, sex, and motor severity (hazard ratio per one-standard-deviation increase, 0.740; 95% confidence interval, 0.613-0.894; p = 0.002). Restricted cubic splines showed evidence of a nonlinear association (p < 0.001), with risk rising disproportionately at lower binding; relative to the median, the adjusted hazard was 2.52 (95% confidence interval, 1.72-3.69) at the 5th percentile. papers.title: Failure of a device-aided therapy in Parkinson's disease, what's next?
papers.abstract: Advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) frequently progresses to disabling motor fluctuations, dyskinesias, and impaired quality of life despite optimized oral or transdermal therapy. Device-aided therapies (DAT), including deep brain stimulation (DBS), levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), levodopa-entacapone-carbidopa intestinal gel (LECIG), continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (CSAI), continuous subcutaneous levodopa-carbidopa infusion (SCLC), and foslevodopa-foscarbidopa infusion (FLFC), provide effective management options for advanced PD. This narrative review discusses discontinuation rates, causes of treatment cessation, and switching between DATs. DBS consistently demonstrates the lowest discontinuation rates, while pump-based therapies, particularly subcutaneous infusions, show higher early dropout rates related to adverse events, device complications, neuropsychiatric symptoms, skin reactions, or insufficient efficacy. Intestinal levodopa therapies generally show intermediate persistence rates, although device-related complications remain common. Emerging evidence suggests that education, clinical experience, and structured patient support may reduce discontinuation from newer subcutaneous levodopa as well as apomorphine therapies. Patients who discontinue one DAT remain eligible for another. Shared decision-making and multidisciplinary evaluation remain essential to optimize long-term outcomes and treatment persistence in advanced PD. Future prospective comparative studies are needed to standardize DAT selection, clarify optimal switching strategies, and improve long-term treatment retention rates in patients.

papers.title: Validation of the English Version of the Parkinson's Disease Quality of Life-7 Questionnaire.
Euthanasia requests in Dutch people with Parkinsonian disorders: a qualitative study on the experiences of healthcare professionals.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: In the Netherlands, over 60,000 individuals live with Parkinson's disease (PD) and atypical parkinsonism (AP). As these chronic diseases progress, treatment goals gradually shift toward palliative care. This transition includes conversations among healthcare professionals (HCP), people with AP/PD, and informal caregivers, known as Advance Care Planning (ACP). Some individuals consider euthanasia or physician assisted suicide (PAS). Euthanasia and PAS is legally possible in the Netherlands since 2002 under The Termination of Life on Request and Assisted Suicide Act, provided that strict legal criteria are met. After euthanasia, the procedures are subject to review by regional euthanasia review committees. However, it is unclear when HCP consider ACP conversations appropriate, how they view euthanasia and PAS in AP/PD, and how they experience euthanasia requests. Some hesitate because cognitive decline in patients might be involved. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to understand Dutch HCP experiences with ACP and euthanasia and PAS requests in people with AP/PD and explores their thoughts, feelings, and opinions when confronted with requests for euthanasia or PAS. METHOD: We conducted a qualitative study using eight closed and open questions focused specifically on experience with requests among HCP that volunteered to participate after completing a blended learning program on palliative care. HCP were also invited through announcements by professional organizations. RESULTS: Sixty respondents completed the questionnaire. Half were elderly care physicians, followed by neurologists and nurse practitioners involved in AP/PD care. One quarter had recently cared for a person with AP/PD who died, and over one-third had received at least one euthanasia request. papers.title: Objective Predictors of Visual Quality of Life in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The goal was to identify drivers of visual disability in Parkinson's disease (PD). METHODS: Participants with PD (n = 25) and controls (n = 11) completed the National Eye Institute Visual Function Questionnaire (VFQ-25) and the Convergence Insufficiency Symptom Survey (CISS), underwent ophthalmologic examination, and high-resolution binocular eye tracking of vergence and gaze-holding. Predictive models were evaluated using clinic-only and combined clinic + eye-tracking approaches. RESULTS: PD participants had lower VFQ-25, higher CISS scores, and the deficits centered on near activities and mental health. Eye tracking showed delayed vergence initiation, reduced gain, and greater gaze instability. Near-point convergence (NPC) and eye-tracking metrics correlated with VFQ-25 and CISS scores. Predictive performance was evident with clinical measures alone and improved with added eye-tracking variables. CONCLUSIONS: Visual disability in PD is strongly linked to convergence insufficiency and gaze instability. NPC, particularly when paired with eye tracking, may be a practical marker of patient-reported visual outcomes. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Investigation of Parkinsonism-Associated Genes in a Large Cohort of Individuals with Early-Onset or Familial Predominant Parkinsonism.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: A study of a large cohort, including early-onset or familial patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), has deciphered the contribution of known PD genes. However, many other genes, thereafter labeled parkinsonism-associated genes (PAG), are associated with other neurological conditions in which parkinsonism is sometimes reported. OBJECTIVE: The aim was to evaluate the contribution of these genes in patients with predominant parkinsonism. METHODS: We performed whole-exome sequencing in a cohort of 1488 probands with early-onset (here defined by an age at onset <45) or familial predominant parkinsonism (1756 in total) who did not have a pathogenic variant in seven known PD genes (GBA1, LRRK2, PARK7, PINK1, PRKN, SNCA, VPS35). One hundred eighteen PAGs were selected for the analysis based on their assessment by experts in three different consortia (Genomics England PanelApp, PanelApp Australia, International Genetic Nomenclature in Movement Disorders Study Group). Pathogenic variants were extracted from these genes according to the criteria of the American College of Medical Genetics. RESULTS: Eighty-one probands (5.4%) carried a pathogenic variant of one PAG. Clinical review (available for 71/81 probands) revealed that the phenotype was compatible with the variant in 91.5% (65/71) of probands. Thirty-seven genes were considered disease causing. Among them, six (ATP13A2, ATXN2, FIG4, GCH1, PLA2G6, PPP2R5D) accounted for a large proportion of probands with a compatible phenotype (26/65, 40.0%). CONCLUSIONS: Our results indicate that PAGs would account for about 5% of patients with early-onset or familial predominant parkinsonism not mutated for known PD genes, and that clinical evaluation is essential to establish causality. © 2026 The Author(s). papers.title: Intercellular Mitochondrial Transfer in Parkinson's Disease: Cargo Quality, Cell State Vulnerability, and Therapeutic Selectivity.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is still often framed as a neuron-autonomous defect of vulnerable dopaminergic neurons. This view misses an intercellular layer of mitochondrial quality control in which glia, extracellular vesicles, tunnelling nanotubes, and mitochondrial extrusion pathways influence whether mitochondrial material is retained, degraded, transferred, or released. In acute CNS injury, mitochondrial transfer can restore bioenergetic capacity in stressed cells. In PD, the same process is unlikely to be uniformly protective. PINK1/Parkin, LRRK2, GBA1, and α-synuclein affect mitochondrial quality control, organelle trafficking, vesicle biology, lysosomal clearance, and innate immune activation. These changes create conditions in which transferred cargo may be beneficial, disposable, or harmful. Here, we distinguish direct PD evidence from mechanisms inferred from other CNS disorders and general cell biology. We interpret mitochondrial transfer in PD through two linked variables: cargo quality and recipient cell state. Functional mitochondria may support metabolic repair; damaged organelles may be routed for disposal; and α-synuclein- or mtDNA-associated cargo may propagate proteopathic stress and inflammation. Therapeutic strategies should therefore focus less on increasing mitochondrial movement per se than on enriching competent cargo, preserving donor cell fitness, and preventing transfer routes from amplifying pathology.

papers.title: Dual kinase inhibition provides early clues to restoration of neuroimmune homeostasis in an AAV-haSyn model of Parkinsons disease.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: Background Previous studies of drugs targeting mixed linage kinase type 3 (MLK3) and/or leucine rich repeat kinase type 2 (LRRK2) in sporadic Parkinsons disease (PD) have failed to meet clinical endpoints despite multiple lines of evidence implicating these kinases in pathogenesis. This has reduced enthusiasm for MLK3 and LRRK2 as druggable targets. Largely overlooked is the evidence that these targets remain valid but must be considered in combination to achieve a therapeutic outcome. This provides the rationale for this study. Methods We conducted a pilot study modeling early, pre-symptomatic PD with subsequent evaluation of therapeutic potential of a multi-kinase inhibitor (URMC-099) in alleviating disease pathology. Sprague Dawley rats received unilateral intranigral injections of low dose AAV-haSyn. After a two-week recovery period, all animals were administered either once-daily intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of URMC-099 or its vehicle control until their terminal endpoint. Induction of early PD, and its alleviation with URMC-099, was evaluated by lateralized motor impairment using the cylinder test and immunohistochemical analysis of neuropathology in the substantia nigra (SN) and striatum. Finally, an in vitro microglial PD model exposed to aSyn pre-formed fibrils and treated with URMC-099 was used to further evaluate the mechanism underlying therapeutic activity. Results A unilateral model of early and progressive AAV-haSyn model for PD was used to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of a targeted multi-kinase inhibitor to attenuate PD-associated neuropathology and prevent the manifestation of lateral motor deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed protection of neuronal cellular integrity along the nigral-striatal pathway with once-daily i.p. URMC-099.
